text: dsh-ptc-moejs 是 DSH 插件，为 PTC 模式提供基于 Go 实现的 moejs JavaScript 程序运行时。它注册为可切换的 PTC runtime，并通过长驻 sidecar 执行模型生成的程序。主要能力包括调用 DSH 工具、设置运行时限与内存和输出预算、使用定时器与部分 Node 模块，以及按文件策略隔离 sidecar。适合希望以此运行时执行 PTC 程序的 DSH 用户；需安装对应平台的可选二进制包并在 profile 中启用。

dsh-ptc-moejs adds a moejs JavaScript runtime for DSH PTC. It runs model-written programs in a reusable sidecar, with DSH tool bindings, timers, selected Node modules, and time, memory, and output budgets. The sidecar follows the file policy. Install its platform binary and enable it in the profile.
想让 DSH 的 PTC 程序用 Go 实现的 JavaScript 引擎运行
希望 PTC 执行时复用 sidecar，减少每次启动运行时的开销
需要给模型生成的程序设置运行时限和内存预算
想让 PTC 程序通过 DSH 提供的工具完成操作
需要在 DSH PTC 运行中使用定时器和部分 Node 模块
想按会话文件策略约束 PTC 运行时进程
I want DSH PTC programs to run on a Go-based JavaScript engine
I need a persistent sidecar runtime for model-written PTC programs
dsh-ptc-moejs 的功能「PTC 程序运行」：将模型生成的程序交给 moejs runtime，在长驻 sidecar 中执行；每次运行创建新的 JavaScript runtime，并返回运行结果。
dsh-ptc-moejs 的功能「工具调用」：程序可调用 DSH 绑定的工具；sidecar 将调用及参数交给宿主，宿主执行绑定后把结果回复给程序。
dsh-ptc-moejs 的功能「运行预算」：为运行配置时限、内存、日志、返回值、并发调用和定时器预算；超限会产生相应运行错误。
dsh-ptc-moejs 的功能「沙箱运行」：sidecar 按解析出的文件策略启动，并可复用同一策略对应的 sidecar 进程。
dsh-ptc-moejs 的功能「平台二进制选择」：按操作系统和架构解析可选 sidecar 包；支持 macOS、Linux 和 Windows x64 平台。
dsh-ptc-moejs README · Introduction：

dsh-ptc-moejs README · dsh-ptc-moejs：A PTC runtime for the DeepSeek Harness that runs the model's programs in moejs, a JavaScript engine written in Go.

简体中文 | English

dsh-ptc-moejs README · dsh-ptc-moejs：In the PTC mode of the [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (dsh), the model answers with a TypeScript program that calls tools. This runtime runs each program in a fresh [moejs](https://github.com/Calcium-Ion/moejs) runtime inside a sidecar process that stays up between programs. A program with three tool calls takes 0.4 ms here, and 110 ms on dsh's Node runtime, which starts a Node process for every program.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · dsh-ptc-moejs：Programs can wait on timers, import helper modules from the working directory and use `node:path`, `node:util` and `node:timers`, and dsh's workflow tool runs its scripts here too.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · dsh-ptc-moejs：Everything a program does to the machine is a tool call, which dsh runs with that tool's own policy, approvals and sandbox. The sidecar itself only reads the code files a program imports, and it gets the confinement dsh's Node runtime gives a program: the file sandbox of the Session's policy and the same short environment. A run stops at its deadline, even in an endless loop, and when it goes past its memory budget.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Performance：Both runtimes ran the same program through dsh's `PtcRuntime` service API, mounted on dsh's own services: three tool calls, each answered at once by its binding, and a returned object.

| Runtime | Per call | Load to first result |
|---|--:|--:|
| dsh-ptc-moejs, workspace-write | 0.42 ms | 16.4 ms |
| dsh-ptc-moejs, danger-full-access | 0.42 ms | 6.8 ms |
| dsh-ptc-runtime-node, workspace-write | 110.4 ms | 164.4 ms |
| dsh-ptc-runtime-node, danger-full-access | 103.0 ms | 149.2 ms |

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Performance：A call is one `resolve` and `run`, from the program text to the result. Workspace-write is the default file policy of a dsh Session, under which both runtimes start their process inside bubblewrap: the Node runtime one process per program, moejs one sidecar for many programs. Danger-full-access starts the process directly. Load to first result runs from mounting the plugin to the end of its first run, and for moejs it includes starting the sidecar.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Performance：Every round started each runtime in a fresh Node process. The 5 rounds alternated the order of the runtimes on an Intel Core i5-13500H, with Linux 6.18, Node 24.22.1, Go 1.26.6, dsh 0.2.1-rc.2 and moejs v0.1.0-alpha.9. The table gives the median of the round medians, which stayed within 0.37 to 0.46 ms for moejs and within 100 to 114 ms for Node.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · A long agent conversation：`bench/agent.mjs` runs one conversation in a headless dsh on each runtime. A scripted model makes 40 `run_code` calls over a copy of five dsh packages, and the programs make 90 calls to dsh's tools: glob, read, grep and bash. Both runtimes ran under workspace-write on the same machine. The table gives the average of 3 conversations on each runtime.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · A long agent conversation：| | dsh-ptc-runtime-node | dsh-ptc-moejs |
|---|--:|--:|
| `run_code` time | 8.6 s | 3.6 s |
| of which the nested tool calls | 3.5 s | 3.3 s |
| Wall time of the conversation | 10.1 s | 5.0 s |
| CPU time of dsh and its child processes | 8.4 s | 5.2 s |
| Peak memory (PSS) of dsh and its child processes | 440 MiB | 437 MiB |
| Peak memory (PSS) of the PTC runtime's processes | 34.0 MiB | 18.5 MiB |
| Processes of the PTC runtime, bubblewrap's included | 120 | 3 |

dsh-ptc-moejs README · A long agent conversation：Each program took 125 ms less on moejs, between 89 and 159 ms depending on the program, and used 82 ms less CPU time. No program was slower. The tool calls take about as long on both runtimes. The difference is the Node process that the Node runtime starts inside bubblewrap for every program. Memory peaks at about the same level on both runtimes, and the dsh process itself makes up about 385 MiB of that peak. The Node runtime's process for each program reaches 34 MiB and exits with the program. The moejs sidecar and its bubblewrap processes stay up for the whole conversation and peak at 18.5 MiB.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · A day of agent work：The saving grows with the number of programs. The scripted model answers at once, and a real model's time per step adds the same on both runtimes, so the saving is the time an agent spends waiting for its programs. The table multiplies the measured 125 ms and 82 ms of CPU time per program by the programs of a day. The examples assume one program every 10 seconds.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · A day of agent work：| Programs a day | For example | Waiting saved | CPU time saved |
|--:|---|--:|--:|
| 200 | half an hour of agent work | 25 s | 16 s |
| 1,000 | about 3 hours | 2.1 min | 1.4 min |
| 2,880 | one agent busy for 8 hours | 6.0 min | 3.9 min |
| 11,520 | four such agents in parallel | 24 min | 16 min |

The busy agent spends 10.3 minutes of its 8 hours in `run_code` on the Node runtime and 4.3 minutes on moejs. For your own estimate, multiply the programs your agents run in a day by 125 ms.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Every effect is a tool call：A program can call the tools dsh gives it and write to `console`. To read a file, run a command or fetch a page, it calls a tool, and dsh runs that call through its tool pipeline with the tool's own policy, approvals and sandbox, as it does for the Node runtime. dsh's session log records each call. The one thing the sidecar reads itself is a code file that the program imports, under the sandbox of the run's policy.
section: Every effect is a tool call

text: dsh-ptc-moejs README · The Node runtime's sandbox：The sidecar runs under the same confinement as the Node runtime's program process:

dsh-ptc-moejs README · The Node runtime's sandbox：- The policy is the one dsh resolves for the run: the Session's file mode and its workspace root, or the deployment's default for a run without a Session.
- dsh's sandbox service confines the sidecar with its runner for the host: bubblewrap or Landlock on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS, the restricted-token runner on Windows. Danger-full-access starts the sidecar without one.
- A restricted mode fails closed. When no runner can confine the sidecar, the run fails with `sandbox-unavailable`, as it does on the Node runtime, so a container where neither bubblewrap nor Landlock works needs danger-full-access.
- Of the dsh process's environment, the sidecar keeps only `PATH`, `PATHEXT`, `SYSTEMROOT`, `WINDIR`, `TEMP` and `TMP`, the variables the Node runtime keeps, and `ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE`, so dsh Desktop's Electron can run the Windows sandbox runner. API keys stay out of it.
- A change of a Session's file mode stops that Session's runs under the old mode.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · The Node runtime's sandbox：On Linux the plugin opens the sidecar's binary itself and the sandboxed sidecar runs from that open file, so it starts even where the sandbox hides the binary's directory, as bubblewrap hides /tmp under workspace-write. `ps` lists such a sidecar as `/proc/self/fd/3`.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · The Node runtime's sandbox：Each file policy in use has its own sidecar, which Sessions with the same mode and workspace root share. The sandbox applies to the sidecar process. Apart from reading the files it imports, the program has no file, network or process access of its own, so the policy decides what a tool call may do, not what the program does.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · The Node runtime's sandbox：The plugin starts the sandboxed command itself. dsh's subprocess service, which starts the Node runtime's processes, also puts each one in a systemd scope behind a Node bootstrap on Linux, so that it can reap the child processes a program leaves behind. That adds about 80 ms to a start, and the sidecar starts no child processes. The sidecar always runs on the host that runs dsh: in a deployment whose execution world is another host, such as one over SSH, a restricted mode fails with `sandbox-unavailable`.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · A fresh runtime for every run：The sidecar of the default policy starts when the plugin loads, and each sidecar keeps running between programs. It exits after five minutes without runs, and the next run starts it again. Each run gets its own moejs runtime, so every program starts from clean globals, and one sidecar can have several runs in flight at once.
section: A fresh runtime for every run

text: dsh-ptc-moejs README · Limits on every run：A run may allocate 512 MiB by default, garbage included. A deadline, an abort from dsh or a profile shutdown stops a run at once. Console output, the returned value and each message to the sidecar have their own size caps, listed under [Configuration](#configuration).

dsh-ptc-moejs README · TypeScript as on the Node runtime：Programs are TypeScript with erasable syntax, the rule dsh's Node runtime applies: the types are removed, and `enum`, namespaces with values and parameter properties are syntax errors. A program is the body of an async function, so `await` and `return` work at its top level.
section: TypeScript as on the Node runtime

text: dsh-ptc-moejs README · Timers：`setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate` and their clear functions work as they do in Node, with `Timeout` objects that have `ref`, `unref`, `hasRef`, `refresh` and `close`, and `node:timers/promises` gives their promise forms. A program can wait between tool calls, poll or retry with a backoff:

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Timers：Timer callbacks run in the program's runtime, so they count toward its memory budget and its deadline. Timers that are still pending when the program returns never run, as the Node runtime's process ends with the program.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Modules：- `.ts`, `.mts`, `.js` and `.mjs` files of the working directory, named with their extension by a path relative to it, an absolute path or a `file:` URL. An imported module can import other files with `import` declarations and use `console` and the timers. It gets the tool bindings from the program, as arguments.
- `node:path`, `node:util`, `node:timers`, `node:timers/promises` and `node:vm`, also without the `node:` prefix.
- `data:` URLs of JavaScript.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Modules：The sidecar reads an imported file itself, under the run's sandbox, and compiles it once for each content it has: a later run that imports the same unchanged file skips the compile. A path outside the working directory, a symbolic link that leads out of it, a package name, a JSON file and the other Node modules fail with an error that says why. Files load only when dsh's execution world is the host that runs dsh. Where it is another host, such as one over SSH, the built-in modules still load.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Workflows：dsh's workflow tool runs on this runtime. Its guest loads from a `data:` URL and runs each workflow script through `node:vm`, which runs the script in the program's own runtime, with the context's properties as its global names. The scripts call `agent()`, `parallel()`, `pipeline()`, `phase()` and `log()` as they do on the Node runtime.
dsh-ptc-moejs README · One static binary：The sidecar is a self-contained Go binary built with `CGO_ENABLED=0`. The package manager installs the binary for your platform as an optional dependency.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Differences from the Node runtime：Programs get the JavaScript standard library, the tools, Node's timers and five Node modules: `node:path`, `node:util`, `node:timers`, `node:timers/promises` and `node:vm`. `require`, `process`, `Buffer`, `fs`, packages and the other Node modules are not available, and a program that needs the content of a file asks the `read` tool for it. If your programs use other Node APIs, keep dsh's Node runtime for that profile.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Differences from the Node runtime：On the Node runtime, `import("./helper.ts")` in a program resolves against dsh's own bootstrap file, so programs there import files by their absolute path. Both forms work here, and a relative path resolves against the working directory.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Differences from the Node runtime：`node:vm` runs a script in the program's own runtime. The `timeout` option of a script is not enforced, and the run's deadline stops a script that does not end. The `var` and `function` declarations of a script stay in the script, and an assignment to a name the context does not have creates a global of the program's runtime, where Node puts both on the context. A workflow that loops forever therefore ends as a `timeout` of its `run_code` call, where the Node runtime reports the script's own timeout. Stack frames of such a script name `node:vm` instead of the script's file name.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Differences from the Node runtime：`run_code` takes `sandbox_permissions` and `justification` as it does on the Node runtime, and an approved request runs the program in a sidecar under the wider mode. Apart from reading the files it imports, the program does no file access of its own, so that approval lets it do nothing more. When the file sandbox denies a tool call, the program retries that call with `sandbox_permissions` and `justification` among its arguments, and you approve each such call. On the Node runtime, an approval for `run_code` also covers the file operations a program does itself through Node APIs.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Quick start：```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-ptc-moejs
```

Use the name of the profile you run in place of `web`. The sidecar binary comes as an optional dependency for darwin-arm64, darwin-x64, linux-arm64, linux-x64 and win32-x64, so install with optional dependencies enabled.

Installing adds a disabled `ptc-moejs` row to the profile. To select it, add this patch to the profile's `cordis.patch.yml`, which is `~/.dsh/profiles/<name>/cordis.patch.yml` (or the same path under `$DSH_HOME`):

```yaml

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Replace the Node PTC runtime with moejs.：- id: ptc-runtime
  disabled: true
- id: ptc-moejs
  disabled: false
section: Replace the Node PTC runtime with moejs.

text:
dsh-ptc-moejs README · Turn PTC mode on.：- id: tools
  config:
    mode: ptc
```

`dsh --profile web --dump-config` prints the composed rows. In the web and headless profiles, `DSH_TOOLS_MODE=ptc` also turns PTC mode on for one launch, in place of the `tools` entry. To go back to the Node runtime, delete the first two entries.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Configuration：Options go on the `ptc-moejs` row of the same patch:

```yaml
- id: ptc-moejs
  disabled: false
  config:
    memoryLimitMb: 1024

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Configuration：| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|--:|---|
| `timeoutMs` | 120000 | Deadline of a run in milliseconds when the model asks for none. Tool calls and approvals count toward it. |
| `maxTimeoutMs` | 600000 | The longest deadline a run may ask for. |
| `memoryLimitMb` | 512 | MiB a run may allocate over its whole life, garbage included. Past it the run stops with `timeout` and a message that names the budget. |
| `maxLogBytes` | 16 MiB | Bytes of console output a run keeps, counted as the JSON array dsh stores. Output past it is dropped, a marker line ends the logs, and the run goes on. |
| `maxValueBytes` | 16 MiB | Bytes of the returned value as JSON. A larger value fails the run with `output-limit`. Error messages are cut to this size. |
| `maxPendingCalls` | 128 | Tool calls a run may have in flight at once. One more fails the run with `protocol`. |
| `maxPendingTimers` | 65536 | Timers and immediates a run may have pending at once. One more throws a `RangeError` in the program. |
| `maxFrameBytes` | 64 MiB | The largest message between dsh and the sidecar: a program, the arguments of a tool call or one tool result. A larger tool result reaches

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Configuration：The deadline defaults follow dsh's Node runtime. dsh spills tool results longer than 12,500 tokens to a file, so the log and value budgets are limits on memory use.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · What a program sees：A program is the body of an async function. Its parameters are the binding namespaces dsh passes (`tools` in PTC mode), the error class of each namespace (`ToolCallError`, which carries the tool's name in `toolName`) and `console` with `log`, `info`, `warn`, `error` and `debug`. `console` is also a global, as are `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `setImmediate` and their clear functions, so the modules a program imports can use them; the binding namespaces are not. The rest is the JavaScript standard library, which in moejs includes `TextEncoder`, `TextDecoder`, `atob`, `btoa`, `structuredClone` and `queueMicrotask`.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · What a program sees：The returned value goes back to dsh as lossless JSON: plain objects, arrays, strings, finite numbers, booleans and `null`. A value that holds `undefined`, a function, a `BigInt`, a cycle, `NaN`, `Infinity`, `-0`, a `Date`, a `Map` or a class instance fails the run with `invalid-output`, and the message gives the path of the first such member, for example `a BigInt at $.items[3].size`. A program that returns nothing completes with no value. Tool arguments follow the same rule, and a call with arguments that are not lossless JSON rejects inside the program before dsh sees it.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · What a program sees：| Failure kind | When |
|---|---|
| `exception` | The program or a timer callback throws, a promise rejects and nothing handles it, the program has a syntax error, or it uses TypeScript that changes run-time behaviour, such as `enum`. |
| `timeout` | The deadline passes, or the program allocates more than `memoryLimitMb`. |
| `abort` | dsh cancels the run, the profile shuts the runtime down, or the Session's file mode changes. |
| `invalid-output` | The returned value is not lossless JSON. |
| `output-limit` | The returned value is larger than `maxValueBytes`. |
| `protocol` | More than `maxPendingCalls` tool calls are in flight, or the sidecar sent a malformed message. |
| `sandbox-unavailable` | The file mode needs a sandbox and no runner on this host can confine the sidecar, or the runner failed before the sidecar ran. |
| `worker-exit` | The sidecar process died or could not start. The next run starts a new one. |

dsh-ptc-moejs README · What a program sees：A result also carries the facts of the sandbox the sidecar ran in, as on the Node runtime: the mode and, under a restricted mode, whether the runner enforces it fully or in part.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Limitations：- Every call starts with a fresh runtime. A persistent mode that keeps variables between calls, like the Node runtime's REPL mode, is planned for a later version.
- The memory budget counts what a run allocates, garbage included. A long run that builds and drops a lot of data can stop before its live data reaches the budget.
- Values nest up to 10,000 levels deep in both directions, the depth moejs's JSON reader and writer handle.
- `console` renders values with a port of Node 22's `util.inspect`, with the options dsh's Node runtime gives it: depth 4, 100 items and 10,000 characters of a string. Node 24 writes the symbol keys of an object without brackets. Node's `util.inspect` shows a proxy's target with `showProxy`, and the entries of an iterator and of a `WeakMap`, which moejs does not expose.
- A run imports at most 256 files, each up to 1 MiB and 8 MiB in all. moejs has no import attributes, so JSON modules are not available. The program is the body of a function, so it imports with `import()`, and `import` declarations work in the modules it imports.

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Development：```sh
pnpm install
pnpm run build:sidecar   # the sidecar for this machine, into npm/<package>/bin
pnpm run build           # lib/
pnpm test                # unit tests and the behaviour suite against the sidecar, on dsh's own services

dsh-ptc-moejs README · Development：Building the sidecar takes Go 1.25 or later, with `CGO_ENABLED=0`. The tests mount dsh's fs, sandbox and policy packages, and one of them runs a program under this host's sandbox when a runner is usable. `DSH_REPO` is a dsh checkout after `pnpm install` and `pnpm run build`. The e2e test installs this checkout into a temporary profile with `dsh plugin add`, runs one headless task in which the mock model calls `run_code`, and compares the Session log, with the `run_code` parameters the model was offered, against the same task on the Node runtime. `compare` runs about a hundred programs on this runtime and on the Node runtime and prints a Markdown report of where their logs, values and failures differ.
